blokken: AI and BI: the difference, and how they strengthen each other

AI and BI are often used interchangeably, but they answer different questions. Business intelligence shows what happened; AI helps predict, explain and unlock information that doesn't fit in a table. Here's the difference, how AI strengthens BI, and why a solid BI foundation is often the best starting point for AI.
Read more on AI for business → See the AI Readiness Assessment →
Written by Dave Willemstein, independent AI consultant · published October 27, 2026
BI describes and explains the past using structured data; AI predicts, classifies and also works with text.
AI in BI tools is only as good as the data model underneath: clear definitions come before clever features.
A working BI environment with trusted numbers is often the best starting point for AI.

What's the difference between AI and BI, and how do they complement each other?

BI mostly works with structured data and shows what happened and why; AI predicts, classifies and also handles text and documents, with a margin of error you need to know. AI and BI aren't competitors: AI builds on the reliable numbers and definitions that BI delivers. A working BI environment with trusted numbers is therefore often the best starting point for AI.
In how many ways can AI be used for business intelligence?

Four ways, from simple to far-reaching: asking questions in plain language, automatic commentary on numbers and anomalies, predictions alongside the usual look back, and turning text from emails, customer feedback and documents into analysable data. For AI and BI, all four rest on a reliable data model.
Is the output of AI as exact as that of BI?

No, BI's output is exact, provided the data is correct, while an AI model estimates and makes mistakes while doing so. For AI and BI, that calls for a different way of checking and a different conversation about accountability.
Source: article by Dave Willemstein. Updated: October 2026.

Business intelligence, or BI for short, is the process of collecting, structuring and visualising business data so you can make decisions on it. Think dashboards showing revenue by region, reports on stock and margin, or a monthly overview for the management team.

Underneath the dashboards sits the real work: bringing data together from different systems, cleaning it up and agreeing what a term actually means. What counts as a customer, when does an order count as revenue, how is margin calculated? BI runs on structured data in tables, and on fixed, repeatable questions: what happened, and why?
Good BI means everyone in the organisation is talking about the same numbers. That sounds simple, but it’s often the hardest part.

AI, artificial intelligence, is an umbrella term for systems that learn patterns from data and use them to carry out tasks that previously needed human judgement. In a business context, it usually comes in two forms:
Predictive AI (machine learning): models that predict or classify an outcome based on historical data, such as expected demand next month or the likelihood a customer will churn.
Generative AI: language models that understand and produce text. They can summarise documents, answer questions in plain language, and pull information out of emails, contracts or customer feedback.

Where BI mostly works with tables, AI can also handle unstructured information. And where BI looks back, predictive AI looks forward. What AI can mean for organisations more broadly is covered on the AI for business overview page.
The difference between AI and BI
The difference between BI and AI lies in the question they answer, the kind of data they work with, and what you do with the result:
What’s going to happen, what belongs with what, what does this say?
Structured and unstructured: text, documents, images
The person, based on the numbers
The person, with a suggestion or estimate from the system
Exact, provided the data is correct
Probable, with a margin of error you need to know

That last row is the key difference. A BI report calculates: if the data is correct, the output is correct. An AI model estimates, and makes mistakes while doing so. That calls for a different way of checking, and a different conversation about accountability.
So they’re not competitors. BI delivers the reliable numbers and definitions; AI builds on top of them.
Using AI for business intelligence works in four ways, from simple to far-reaching:
Plain-language questionsTyping a question instead of filtering or building a report yourself.
Automatic commentarySummaries and explanations alongside numbers and anomalies.
PredictingLooking ahead at demand, downtime or risk, alongside the usual look back.
New sourcesTurning text from emails, customer feedback and documents into analysable data.
The further down this list you go, the more value, but also the more demands on data, control and governance. All four rest on a reliable data model.

The first two are already built into many BI platforms. One example: Copilot in Power BI lets users ask questions about reports, generate summaries, and helps report authors build pages and calculations. Microsoft itself notes that without preparing the data model, Copilot can misread the data and give generic or incorrect answers. It also requires paid Fabric or Premium capacity; a Pro licence alone isn’t enough (as of September 2026, according to Microsoft Learn).

That illustrates the point: AI in BI is only as good as the foundation underneath it. Unclear column names, three different definitions of “revenue”, and missing descriptions all lead to answers that sound convincing but aren’t correct. How to build that foundation around concrete applications, rather than trying to get everything in order first, is something I wrote about in the data foundation under AI.
A few recognisable ways AI and BI come together:
Management reporting with commentary. The monthly report is supplemented with a plain-language summary of the main variances, which the controller checks and adds to.
Demand forecasting. Alongside last year’s sales figures, the dashboard shows a forecast for the coming weeks, as input for purchasing and planning.
Customer feedback as data. Reviews, complaints and emails are automatically categorised by topic and tone, so you can set them alongside your revenue and returns figures.
Asking your own questions. A sales manager asks in plain language which customers are ordering less than last quarter, without waiting for a new report.
Flagging anomalies. Unusual bookings or sudden changes in a series are flagged for a human check.

For smaller businesses, this usually starts with the AI features already in the BI or accounting package they use; see also AI for small business. At professional services firms, the emphasis is more often on unlocking documents than on dashboards.

A retail chain with 35 stores and a two-person BI team wants to roll out Copilot in Power BI so eight regional managers can ask their own questions about revenue and margin. The consultant first tests 50 questions the regional managers actually ask against the existing data model.

Of those 50 answers, 19 are wrong. The cause isn't the AI: there are three different definitions of margin in circulation, and many column names say nothing useful. Over six weeks, the BI team documents clear definitions and descriptions for the twenty most-used terms. On a second test against the same questions, 44 of 50 are correct.
Deliberately not done: opening the feature up to all 120 report users straight away. The rollout starts with the eight regional managers, with a monthly spot-check by the BI team.
Illustrative example, built from situations that come up often. The organisation and figures are for illustration.

Where do I fit into this? I’m not a BI builder. I don’t build dashboards or set up data warehouses. My role sits ahead of and above that: helping decide which AI applications on your data create value, what needs to happen to the foundation first, and which party can deliver it. I do that as part of my AI consulting. For the delivery itself, your own BI team or a party from my partner network, whom you contract directly, does the work.

Want to know what the BI role itself actually involves and how it’s changing? A separate article on this site covers what a BI specialist does. Not sure whether your question belongs with BI, AI or both? Get in touch for a short conversation.
Independent: no commissions, no partner deals, no margin on implementation partners.

Not entirely. Fixed dashboards stay useful for the numbers you want to see the same way every week. AI does make it easier to look beyond those fixed questions, for example by asking something in plain language. You'll likely need fewer dashboards, but a better set of core metrics.
Do we need BI in order before we start with AI?+

Not for every application. AI for text and documents, such as summarising or sorting email, is largely independent of your BI environment. If you want to use AI for analysis and predictions on your business numbers, you do need clear definitions and reliable data for the figures that application uses.
Can I ask questions about my numbers in plain language?+

A growing number of BI platforms offer that option. Whether the answers are correct depends mainly on how well the underlying data model is set up: clear names, defined terms and documented calculations. Without that groundwork, the feature quickly gives generic or incorrect answers.
Who do I need: a BI specialist, a data scientist or an AI consultant?+

That depends on the question. A BI specialist builds and maintains reports and data models. A data scientist develops predictive models. An AI consultant helps determine which applications create value, which role and party fit, and how to govern it. Smaller organisations often combine an internal BI person with outside support.
